clue.text: A hanging matter to cover Berlin's division?

parts.note: the Berlin Wall divided the city
to paper a surface is to cover it

explanation.surface: A grim question of whether some crime might be covered up along the divided city of Berlin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hanging matter' sounds like a capital crime; it is something decorators hang in strips.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative sheets for interior surfaces are hung by decorators, so the material is literally a hanging matter.

clue.text: One of three who met on the 11

definitions.text: One of three who met on the 11

parts.words: One of three who met on the 11
parts.note: surface reading: one of a trio who met on the eleventh day of some month
setter's reading: 11 refers to the entry 11 across, the heath where the three hags of Macbeth meet

explanation.surface: One of a trio who had a meeting on the eleventh.
explanation.walkthrough: The 11 is a cross-reference to 11 across, HEATH; in Shakespeare's Macbeth the three WITCHes meet upon the heath.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Macbeth opens with three weird sisters gathering on a blasted heath, so each is one of that trio.

clue.text: Sign over railway book store?

parts.note: Libra, the scales, is a sign of the zodiac
RY is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A signal mounted above a railway line, perhaps outside a station bookshop.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means the first piece sits above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A place where volumes are kept and lent out is literally a store of reading matter, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Not the right openings for those who go to sea?

definitions.text: openings for those who go to sea

parts.note: port is the nautical left, the side that is not the right
holes are openings

explanation.surface: A careers adviser's warning that these are the wrong opportunities for would-be sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Openings' does double duty: it supplies the second piece and is the heart of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors' cabins have small round glazed windows set in the hull, letting light and air in at sea.

clue.text: Not where a gardener goes for target practice

definitions.text: Not where a gardener goes for target practice

parts.note: surface reading: a gardener's hut, where seedlings are put into containers
setter's reading: to pot is also to take a shot at something, so a place for potting sounds like a shooting range

explanation.surface: A joke that the gardener's little hut is not a shooting range.
explanation.walkthrough: To pot means both to plant in a pot and to shoot at game, so the gardener's hut sounds like a firing range.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners keep a small outbuilding where they transfer young plants into containers, named for that potting work.

clue.text: Is associated it Jamaica?

parts.note: surface reading: a question about what is linked with a Caribbean island; setter's reading: the word also means odd or strange
setter's reading: the island is famous for the spirit distilled from sugar cane

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what goes with Jamaica.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue appears garbled in the source; the answer is the spirit Jamaica is known for, and RUM is also British slang for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caribbean island is world-famous for its dark cane spirit, so the drink is closely linked with that place.

clue.text: Science fiction and its strange riddles

indicators.note: strange suggests something made odd or unfamiliar, so the letters are put into an unfamiliar order

parts.note: SF is the standard abbreviation for science fiction
taken as written

explanation.surface: Science fiction and its weird puzzles, the sort of enigmas the genre loves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddles' looks like a noun meaning puzzles, but it is the verb: to riddle is to pass through a coarse sieve.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a coarse sieve, so to riddle soil or gravel is to pass it through a mesh, separating fine from coarse.

clue.text: Will this student get your measure might you say?

indicators.note: asking what you might say points to how a word is spoken rather than how it is written

parts.note: one who sizes you up, or takes your measure, would be a sizer

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a student will size you up, perhaps a tailoring apprentice.
explanation.walkthrough: A SIZAR is an undergraduate at Cambridge or Trinity College Dublin who receives an allowance from the college.
explanation.definitionFit: At some old universities a poorer undergraduate receiving college allowances for food and fees held this title.

clue.text: What's first class about a laminate?

parts.note: Form I is the first class in an old-fashioned school
CA, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: Asking what is so top-quality about a plastic surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First class' looks like a judgement of quality, but in British schools classes were called forms, numbered I, II and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a trade name for the hard plastic sheeting bonded in layers onto kitchen worktops and tables.

clue.text: They float on landings, and keep quiet in main passages

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: the main is the sea, and its passages are shipping routes
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: Instructions for moving discreetly through a building's main corridors, staying quiet on the landings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landings' looks like the parts of a staircase; it means touching down on water. 'The main' is an old word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: These aircraft have floats instead of wheels, so they rest on the water's surface when they touch down.

clue.text: Fabric label to tear out

parts.note: a tab is a small label attached to something

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructions to rip the label out of a piece of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: TABARET is an old upholstery fabric with alternating stripes of satin and watered silk.
explanation.definitionFit: This striped silk furnishing material was used for upholstery and curtains, so it is a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Polish steps to music

parts.note: surface reading: to polish means to shine, so this looks like buffing a staircase
setter's reading: a dance from Poland, performed to music

explanation.surface: Someone buffing the stairs in time to a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P is hidden at the start of the clue: Polish means from Poland, not shine.
explanation.definitionFit: This lively triple-time folk dance originated in Poland and was popularised in Chopin's piano pieces.

clue.text: Erica starts 3 row at the airport

parts.note: surface reading: a woman's name; setter's reading: the botanical genus of low evergreen moorland shrubs
setter's reading: the plant's common name, put before row, begins the name of London's biggest airport

explanation.surface: A woman named Erica kicking off an argument at the airport.
explanation.walkthrough: The source text seems garbled ('3'). HEATH plus ROW makes Heathrow, London's main airport; HEATH is also the common name for plants of the genus Erica.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus of moorland shrubs, and plants of that genus share the common name with open scrubland.

clue.text: Just a mischievous child — a terrible trial

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child; the article comes along with it

indicators.note: something terrible is in a dreadful state, so the following word is wrecked and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Simply that a naughty youngster is an awful ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'simply', but it is the adjective meaning fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A just judge is fair and even-handed, favouring neither side, which is exactly what an unbiased person is.

clue.text: A down-to-earth fighter

parts.note: surface reading: practical and unpretentious; setter's reading: literally coming down to the ground from the sky
setter's reading: a soldier who drops into battle by parachute

explanation.surface: Praise for a sensible, unpretentious combatant.
explanation.definitionFit: These soldiers jump from aircraft and descend under canopies to the ground, literally coming down to earth to fight.

clue.text: Knowing witness to Robin's death

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for sharp, shrewd and street-wise

definitions.note: a noun phrase for an insect, while the answer is also an adjective
definitions.meaning: second meaning: in the nursery rhyme Who Killed Cock Robin, an insect says it saw him die

explanation.surface: A shrewd eyewitness to the killing of someone called Robin.
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme, 'Who saw him die? I, said the Fly, with my little eye.' Fly is also British slang for knowing or sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme insect claims to have seen the bird die, and in slang a fly person is shrewd and alert.

clue.text: An alien " pays " without his right to vote

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: pays is the French word for country, so a foreign pays is that very country
taken as written

explanation.surface: A foreigner pays tax yet has no vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pays' looks like the English verb; the quotation marks flag the French word for country.
explanation.definitionFit: The franchise is the legal entitlement of citizens to cast ballots in elections, also called suffrage.

clue.text: Mere dealing? Sounds " slightly " tricky

indicators.note: dealing suggests cards being shuffled and dealt out in a fresh order

parts.note: both words supply letters, so the second does double duty

explanation.surface: A query whether some trading is a bit shady, sounding slightly dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slightly' sounds like sleight-ly: LEGERDEMAIN is sleight of hand, so the definition describes how it sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Conjurors' sleight of hand is deft trickery, and the quoted word, spoken, sounds like that skill.

clue.text: Contain and brian about

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to surround and hold within
second meaning: a misprint of bring about, cause to happen

explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has a typo; read 'bring about'.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to surround or include something, and in an older sense to achieve or accomplish a goal.

clue.text: A number used locally by dentists

definitions.text: A number used locally by dentists

parts.note: surface reading: a figure, as in arithmetic; setter's reading: something that numbs
setter's reading: dentists inject a local deadening agent before drilling

explanation.surface: Some figure that dental surgeons in a certain area rely on.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'number' as numb-er, a thing that numbs; 'locally' points to a local injection.
explanation.definitionFit: Dentists inject a drug that removes feeling in one area, so it numbs the patient's mouth during treatment.

clue.text: One dreams perhaps of former wonders

definitions.note: an archaic sense of the verb

indicators.note: perhaps hints at a possible version of the word, so its letters may be rearranged

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, then rearranged with the numeral

explanation.surface: A person daydreaming about marvels of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former' marks an old sense: in older English to admire meant to wonder or marvel.
explanation.definitionFit: In earlier English this verb meant to marvel or be astonished, so it once meant the same as wonders.

clue.text: Force 5 is it?

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about a Force 5 wind on the weather scale.
explanation.walkthrough: VIS is the Latin word for force, met in English in phrases like vis inertiae.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin noun for strength or power survives in English technical and legal phrases such as vis major.

clue.text: Make off with Virginia Low's note
Emulate the movements of easy money

definitions.text: Emulate the movements of easy money

parts.note: surface reading: copy how something moves
setter's reading: the saying 'easy come, easy go' describes how readily such cash arrives and departs

explanation.surface: Advice to copy how quickly windfall cash flows.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'easy come, easy go' says money gained easily leaves just as easily.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrive and leave freely is exactly how the proverb says effortlessly gained cash behaves.

clue.text: Danger warning made Capone take Ills gun

parts.note: Al Capone was the Chicago gangster
a gun is an arm, a weapon

explanation.surface: A warning that the gangster has picked up his weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue is garbled in the source; the wordplay is the gangster's first name followed by a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell, siren or signal that alerts people to a threat, such as a fire or burglar warning.

clue.text: Bohemian girl many imitate

parts.note: Mimi is the heroine of Puccini's opera La Bohème
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: Lots of people copying a free-spirited young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian' looks like a free spirit or a Czech; here it points to La Bohème.
explanation.definitionFit: To mimic someone is to copy their voice or manner, a direct verbal synonym of imitate.

clue.text: Conk's province, but Scotland is their land

definitions.text: Conk's province, but Scotland is their land

parts.note: surface reading: a nose's territory; setter's reading: a misprint for a cook's domain, the things a cook bakes
setter's reading: an old poetic nickname for Scotland names it after these baked goods, made there from oats

explanation.surface: A nose's territory contrasted with Scotland as a homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conk' is a misprint for 'Cook'. Burns called Scotland the Land o' Cakes, after its oatcakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Bakers and cooks produce these baked sweet items, and Scotland's old nickname is the Land of Cakes.

clue.text: Encroachments where the Colossus stood, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the spoken form counts rather than the written one

parts.note: the Colossus was the giant statue on the Greek island of Rhodes

explanation.surface: Invasions of the site of the ancient giant statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Making inroads means advancing into territory or eating into something, which is what encroaching does.

clue.text: Place an Egyptian deity

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put down or position
second meaning: the god of chaos and storms in ancient Egypt

explanation.definitionFit: To set a thing is to position it, and Set, also Seth, was the Egyptian god of deserts and disorder.

clue.text: Author proud of his tail-piece?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Thomas Love ..., the English satirical novelist
second meaning: the bird that displays its splendid fan of feathers

explanation.surface: A writer pleased with the closing ornament of his book.
explanation.walkthrough: A tail-piece is a printer's decoration at a chapter's end; here it is the bird's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Love Peacock wrote Nightmare Abbey, and the male bird struts while showing off its iridescent fanned plumage.

clue.text: Where poems are out of place of course

definitions.text: Where poems are out of place of course

indicators.note: letters out of place are displaced, so they must be put back into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A spot where verse naturally doesn't belong.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a racecourse town, where poetry is hardly at home; 'of course' means it has a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: This Surrey town hosts the Derby on its famous racecourse, a place of racing rather than verse.

clue.text: Harvest workers did not spoil their children?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a variant spelling of threshers, who beat grain from the husk

definitions.note: a verb phrase for people who did this, while the answer is a plural noun
definitions.meaning: second meaning: from 'spare the rod and spoil the child', parents who beat their offspring

explanation.surface: Farm labourers who were strict parents.
explanation.walkthrough: THRASHERS is an old spelling of threshers; the proverb 'spare the rod, spoil the child' supplies the other sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmhands beat grain to separate it, and parents who beat their offspring followed the proverb rather than sparing the rod.
